paras: The Vaughanville Odd Fellows hall burning was the destruction of a Black lodge hall at Vaughanville, Newberry County, South Carolina, on the night of October 16, 1903, while about fifty armed white men were gathered nearby. The white men had assembled on a rumor that lodge members had sent for arms and meant to confront Clarence M. Brooks, a white youth who had shot and killed a Black man, Raymond Sizer, the week before. No one was confirmed killed, and the only account found, in the Newberry Herald and News, said the cause of the fire was not known.

Vaughanville lay near the Laurens County line, about twenty-one miles from Newberry; there, on the night of Saturday, October 10, seventeen-year-old Clarence M. Brooks shot and killed Raymond Sizer, and a coroner's jury found that he had acted in self-defense. According to the Herald and News, Black residents refused to touch the body, so white men, among them Brooks's attorney Cole L. Blease, buried it; the next day Black residents dug it up and reburied it about a mile away.

Sizer had been a prominent member of the local Black Odd Fellows lodge, which the paper called a "disturbing element in the community." White residents told the paper's reporter that the lodge had met often and made "numerous threats" since Sizer's death. The paper called this the third threatened race trouble there in recent years, after two Black doctors had been run out of the community.

On the afternoon of October 16 a report circulated that Black residents had sent to Chappells for arms, would meet at the Odd Fellows hall that night, and would then "wait on" Brooks and the white men who had buried Sizer. About four o'clock a telephone call brought a party of twelve from Newberry, with a Herald and News reporter. The reporter found no sign of trouble beyond about thirty-five white men in Whit Goodwyn's store, "armed to the teeth" with shotguns and small arms; with the Newberry party they numbered about fifty.

Blease called a meeting to order, and about nine o'clock a detachment of twelve men went to the Odd Fellows hall, where they found no light and no one present. Shortly after the detachment returned to the store, the hall, a two-story frame building whose ground floor served as a Black school, was seen burning, and it burned to the ground some time before eleven o'clock. The paper stated simply that how the fire started "is not known."

Someone then proposed visiting the supposed ringleaders "to give them correction." Fred H. Dominick opposed it, backed by Blease, Deputy Sheriff Duncan Johnson and Constable C. G. Blease, and it was voted down almost unanimously, the men declaring they had come to protect the white residents and Brooks. The men slept under arms with sentinels posted; nothing further occurred, and most went home the next morning.

No report of an investigation of the fire, or of any arrest connected with the night's events, was found. Brooks came to trial for Sizer's murder in early November; the Herald and News noted that the case had become known throughout the state because of the race trouble at Vaughanville. On November 5, after very little testimony, he was "promptly acquitted."

The only coverage found came from the Herald and News of Newberry, whose reporter rode with the armed party and stayed at the scene overnight. Its front-page report of October 20 ran under the headline "RAGE [Race] TROUBLE WAS SERIOUSLY EXPECTED" and described a threatened "negro uprising." Relying on white residents, it described the hall as a place where members "hatched their schemes without fear of interruption," and it presented the armed men, under the subheading "AN ORDERLY CROWD," as a protective body. It did not speculate on who burned the hall but said that had there been "any demonstration by the negroes" blood "would have been freely spilt."

A report spread in Newberry that a Black man carrying a lantern had been shot dead near the hall. The Herald and News reporter wrote that no such act came to his notice and that the report of a killing appeared unfounded, though he allowed that "some one" may have been fired upon.

bases: About fifty armed white men gathered against a rumored Black lodge meeting, sent a detachment to the lodge hall, and debated punishing alleged ringleaders; the hall burned that night from a cause the paper called unknown, and no one was reported harmed (A3, A4, A5).
All accounts come from one paper, the Newberry Herald and News, in a single front-page report and a later court item (A3, A4, A5, A7); no other paper or Black-press account was found.

accounts.label: White residents of Vaughanville (as told to the reporter)
accounts.gist: The Black Odd Fellows had met often and made numerous threats since Sizer's death, had sent for arms, and intended to call on Brooks and the men who buried Sizer; the lodge had long exercised a 'baneful influence'.

accounts.label: Herald and News reporter (eyewitness)
accounts.gist: Found no sign of trouble beyond the armed white men; the hall was dark and empty, then burned from an unknown cause; no killing came to his notice.

accounts.label: Street rumor in Newberry
accounts.gist: A Black man carrying a lantern near the hall was questioned, said he was a Black man, and was shot dead.

framing.detail: Headlined 'RAGE [Race] TROUBLE WAS SERIOUSLY EXPECTED', called it a threatened 'negro uprising', described the lodge as hatching 'schemes', and presented the armed men as an 'ORDERLY CROWD' come to protect; it did not comment on who burned the hall.

versions.value: A Black man with a lantern was shot and killed near the hall (rumor on the streets of Newberry)
No killing; the reporter at the scene from about 8 p.m. to 7 a.m. saw no such act, though 'some one' may have been fired upon

conflicts.note: Both versions come from the same article; the reporter's account is first-hand but he was traveling with the armed party, and no other report settles it.

record_check.dossier: Armed gathering and a hall burned from a cause the paper says is not known; a proposed punitive visit was voted down. No whipping or forced labor is reported (those appear in an unrelated Charleston peonage item, A6). 'Arson' is not established.
Armed white residents of Vaughanville and a party from Newberry, with a deputy sheriff and constable present; no employer role reported.
The armed gathering is reported with named leaders (Cole L. Blease chaired); who set the fire is unknown.
The Black Odd Fellows lodge (hall destroyed) and the Black community of Vaughanville; five named alleged ringleaders were targeted by a proposal voted down.
One paper only (Newberry Herald and News); the second paper (Sharp County Record) is not about this episode.

record_check.record: Armed white men gathered ... hall burned; cause unknown. A proposed visit to alleged Black ringleaders was voted down.
record_check.dossier: Accurate; add that the gathering followed Clarence M. Brooks's killing of Raymond Sizer on October 10, and that a rumored killing of a Black man near the hall was called unfounded.

info: Friday night, October 16, 1903 (rumor in the afternoon; fire before 11 p.m.)
Vaughanville, upper Newberry County near the Laurens line, about twenty-one miles from Newberry; Whit Goodwyn's store and the Black Odd Fellows hall a quarter mile away

The Black Odd Fellows lodge, whose two-story frame hall (also used as a Black school) burned; five Black men named by local whites as ringleaders (Isaac Fortune, Jones Pitts, West Bates, Jim Wade, Ben Watts) were the object of a proposed visit that was voted down

White residents claimed the lodge had held frequent meetings and made numerous threats since Sizer's death, and a rumor said Black residents had sent to Chappells for arms and would call on Clarence M. Brooks and the men who buried Sizer; the paper's reporter found no meeting and no sign of trouble

Armed white men of Vaughanville, joined by a party of twelve from Newberry; a meeting was chaired by Cole L. Blease; Deputy Sheriff Duncan Johnson and Constable C. G. Blease were present. No one was named as setting the fire.
